newsitem.title: GERMANY: Duisenberg becomes official candidate to head ECB.
newsitem.headline: Duisenberg becomes official candidate to head ECB.

text.p: Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg on Tuesday threw his hat into the ring to head Europe's future central bank, launching an official candidacy for the job.
Duisenberg, slated to become president of the European Monetary Institute this summer, declared his interest in two German newspaper interviews on Tuesday.
"I can make no secret of it, I am a candidate," the Boersen Zeitung quoted Duisenberg as saying, adding that he would be available for an entire first term of eight years.
The European Central Bank will evolve from the European Monetary Institute in 1999 after nations adopt the single currency, the euro.

Germany's Bundesbank has already signalled its backing for Duisenberg in the job. The fact that the Dutch central banker comes from a stability oriented culture is seen reinforcing the European central bank's mandate to ensure price stability.

France on the other hand has recently ruffled diplomatic feathers by intimating that Germany had already agreed to accept a Frenchman for the top job in return for getting the nod to locate the central bank in Frankfurt.
Bundesbank council member Helmut Hesse last week said it would be "completely impossible" that the first head of the planned European Central Bank could be French.
The Bonn Finance Ministry however declined official comment, saying it was premature to begin personnel discussions that were not yet imminent.
In efforts to defuse tensions, Duisenberg stressed no political agreements had been reached between France and Germany and that race was still on.

European government heads will vote on the European central bank president and the directorate members after consultations with the European parliament and the other members of the European Central Bank council.
Those European nations which meet strict entry criteria will be able to join the single currency union in 1999.
